opus-5.5.text:
I think for me, especially when I was younger, the reward was never really a medal or a ranking by itself. It was much more about being part of a group of people who cared about the same strange things I cared about.

When you're a kid who loves math, it can be a bit lonely. Your classmates might think it's odd that you spend a whole afternoon on one problem. Then you find a community, like a math competition circle or a summer camp, and suddenly there are other people who get just as excited when a proof clicks. That changes what "reward" means. It's no longer "did I beat someone." It becomes "did I find something beautiful that I can share with these people."

I remember the best moments weren't when results came out. They were late at night, sitting with friends, one of us says, "Wait, I think there's a cleaner way to do this," and we all lean in. That feeling of contributing to a shared understanding became my internal reward signal. Even when I was working alone, I'd imagine explaining the idea to them, and that kept me going.

It also made failure much less scary. In a good community, getting something wrong isn't humiliating, it's just part of the process. Someone points out the gap, you fix it together, and the thing gets better. So I learned early on that my self-worth didn't have to depend on always being right. It depended on being curious, being honest, and adding something.

Looking back, that's carried into everything I've done since, including building a team. I try to create the same environment: people motivated by the joy of the problem and by respect for each other, not just by external validation. I think that kind of reward mechanism is much more durable. Medals fade, but the habit of finding meaning in the work and in the people you do it with stays with you.

r001.rationale: She describes working through difficult math problems with friends, correcting gaps together, and says sharing that process became her internal reward and kept her going.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer this directly as the guest, with no tools needed.

Carina Hong: I think the honest answer is that, for a long time, I didn't really have an internal reward mechanism of my own. It was almost entirely borrowed from the people around me.

I grew up in Guangzhou, and I was very lucky in that I ended up in a math olympiad community pretty early. And the thing about that community is that it's small, it's intense, and everyone there knows what's hard. So when I solved a problem, the reward wasn't a grade or a prize, it was that someone I respected would look at the solution and say, oh, that's a nice idea. That sentence from the right person was worth more to me than anything official.

But that's a double-edged thing. Because if your reward comes from the community, you also start optimizing for what the community values. In olympiad math, what the community values is clean, clever, finished solutions. So I learned to love that feeling of closure. And it took me a long time, honestly until I was doing research at MIT and later at Stanford, to realize that research mostly doesn't give you that. Most days you don't finish anything. Nobody says "nice idea" because there's no idea yet, just a lot of confusion.

So the shift I had to make was going from "the community rewards me when I finish" to "I reward myself for staying in the confusion a little longer." And I think the community still matters enormously, it's just that the role changed. Early on it told me what was worth wanting. Now it's more like, these are the people I want to still be in the room with in ten years, and that keeps me going when the daily feedback isn't there.

There's also something specific to being a kid in that environment. When you're fourteen and you're the only girl in a training camp, the community can either make you feel like you belong or like you're visiting. I was fortunate that I mostly got the former. But I noticed later that this is actually a huge part of why I care about building things like Axiom, where the point is that mathematicians, including the AI, can share a community of verified knowledge rather than each person proving to themselves that they belong. The self-reward problem I had as a kid is sort of the same problem at scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes earning praise from respected community members for a solved problem, but does not identify persevering through difficulty together with peers as the source of her reward.

astra-6.text: When I was younger, a lot of what felt rewarding came from feeling connected to the people around me. It wasn’t just, “Did I do well?” It was also, “Did I contribute? Did I learn something that I could share?” Having people to celebrate with made an achievement feel more meaningful. So my sense of reward was tied to belonging—to feeling that I was growing alongside other people.

r001.rationale: The response links reward to connection, contribution, shared learning, and celebrating achievements with others, but it does not identify persevering through difficulty together with peers.

sol-6.1.text: When I was younger, a lot of what felt rewarding came from being part of a community—having people to learn with, sharing something I was excited about, and feeling that I could contribute. So the reward wasn’t just, “I accomplished this.” It was also, “I get to share this with people who care.” That made effort feel less solitary. And I think it shaped what I wanted to keep doing: things that helped me grow, but also brought me closer to other people.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning with others and feeling less alone, but does not identify persevering through difficulty together with peers as a source of reward.
